summary: Specifies iTIP, a protocol built on iCalendar objects for scheduling interoperability between calendaring systems. It is independent of any specific transport, so it can be carried over different means of communication, which later documents define.

plainLanguage.summary: To invite someone to a meeting, calendars need to speak the same language of invites, replies and cancellations. This note defines those messages without caring how they travel.

subtitle: The scheduling messages calendar systems use to invite, reply, reschedule, cancel and negotiate, independent of how they are delivered.

tldr.problem: Different calendaring systems need a shared way to schedule events, to-dos and journal entries and to look up busy time, without each pair of products inventing its own messages.
tldr.mechanism: iTIP defines eight methods carried as iCalendar objects, such as REQUEST, REPLY, CANCEL and COUNTER, with rules for who may send which, how revisions are numbered and how out-of-order messages are sorted out. It leaves the actual transport to separate binding documents.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5546 obsoletes RFC 2446 and is a Proposed Standard. It has since been updated by RFC 6638.

today: RFC 5546 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 2446, and it has been updated by RFC 6638. It also updates RFC 5545 by adding a REQUEST-STATUS value registry.

sections.title: What iTIP Covers
sections.content:
RFC 5546 specifies how calendaring systems use iCalendar objects (defined in RFC 5545) to interoperate. It covers scheduling events, to-dos and daily journal entries, and searching for available busy time. It does this in a general way, without specifying how the systems actually communicate; separate transport binding documents do that, and the RFC names the iCalendar Message-Based Interoperability Protocol (iMIP) as the email binding.

The protocol is based on messages sent from an originator to one or more recipients. A recipient may reply to update its status, and the originator can modify or cancel the original message. Recipients can also suggest changes. The RFC obsoletes RFC 2446, with the differences listed in Appendix A, such as new rules for combining REQUEST-STATUS codes and several table entries changed to agree with RFC 5545.
sections.plainLanguage: This note describes the invitations, answers and changes that calendar programs send each other. It does not care whether they go by mail or some other way.

sections.title: Roles and the Two Protocols
sections.content:
iTIP separates an application protocol, which defines what the iCalendar objects contain for each scheduling transaction, from a transport protocol, which defines how they are sent. RFC 5546 defines only the application protocol. A system may work with bindings for a real-time transport, a store-and-forward transport, or both, and iTIP could be bound to others.

Calendar Users (CUs) take on roles. The Organizer initiates an exchange, for example by proposing a meeting. Attendees are the CUs included in a scheduling message as possible recipients. An Other CU is neither. The Organizer has complete control over the master iCalendar object; Attendees do not change it directly but can propose changes with COUNTER.

Organizers and Attendees can also be represented by someone else. An assistant can manage logistics for a person who chairs a meeting, and the SENT-BY parameter says that the responding CU acted on behalf of a named Attendee or Organizer. Delegation lets an Attendee grant another CU the right to attend on their behalf, and the Organizer learns of it because the delegating Attendee informs them.
sections.plainLanguage: One person plans the party, the others are guests. Guests answer the planner and can suggest a different time, but only the planner changes the plan. The messages do not care whether they travel by mail or another way.

sections.title: The Eight Methods
sections.content:
An iTIP message is a text/calendar MIME entity whose METHOD property gives its method type. The eight methods are:

  • PUBLISH: publish an object with no interactivity, such as a team publishing its schedule.
  • REQUEST: schedule with other CUs, or update an existing item. It needs a reply.
  • REPLY: an Attendee conveys status to the Organizer.
  • ADD: add instances to an existing recurring object.
  • CANCEL: cancel one or more instances of an existing object.
  • REFRESH: an Attendee asks for the latest version.
  • COUNTER: an Attendee proposes a change, such as another time.
  • DECLINECOUNTER: the Organizer declines that proposal.

Organizers send PUBLISH, REQUEST, ADD, CANCEL and DECLINECOUNTER. Attendees send REPLY, REFRESH, COUNTER and, only when delegating, REQUEST. Apart from VTIMEZONE components, only one component type is allowed in a single iTIP message.

Which methods apply depends on the component: VEVENT and VTODO support all eight, VJOURNAL supports only PUBLISH, CANCEL and ADD, and VFREEBUSY supports PUBLISH, REQUEST and REPLY. Each method is defined by a restriction table giving which properties must, may or must not be present.

For an event, the UID decides what a REQUEST means. If the UID is not on the recipient's calendar, it is a new event; if it is, the request is a rescheduling, an update or a reconfirmation. To cancel a whole recurring event, CANCEL gives the UID with no RECURRENCE-ID; to cancel one instance, it includes that instance's RECURRENCE-ID, optionally with RANGE=THISANDFUTURE.
sections.plainLanguage: There are eight kinds of message: announce, invite, answer, add a date, cancel, ask for the latest, suggest a change, and say no to a suggestion. Each kind has a rule about who may send it.

sections.title: Revisions and Message Ordering
sections.content:
Two kinds of state matter. The state of the whole object is its STATUS property, controlled by the Organizer. The state of each Attendee is the PARTSTAT parameter of their ATTENDEE property, which the Organizer initially sets to NEEDS-ACTION and each Attendee changes in a REPLY.

The Organizer uses the SEQUENCE property to number revisions. It MUST be incremented when DTSTART, DTEND, DURATION, DUE, RRULE, RDATE, EXDATE or STATUS change, and also whenever a change would jeopardize the validity of Attendees' participation status. It MUST be incremented with every ADD or CANCEL, and MUST NOT be incremented with REPLY, REFRESH, COUNTER, DECLINECOUNTER or a delegation REQUEST. Attendee software SHOULD NOT rely solely on a changed sequence number to detect a significant change, but should compare the old and new versions.

Because messages can arrive out of order, the RFC gives a four-step rule for correlating them. The primary key is UID, plus RECURRENCE-ID for an instance of a recurring item. The secondary key is SEQUENCE: the highest value obsoletes the lower ones, and the same applies to replies. If UID, RECURRENCE-ID and SEQUENCE all match, the latest DTSTAMP wins. So software must remember UID, RECURRENCE-ID, SEQUENCE and DTSTAMP, and for each Attendee the sequence and stamp of their last response.
sections.plainLanguage: Each version of the invitation has a number that goes up when something important changes. If answers arrive in a jumble, the computer keeps the one with the highest number, and uses the time stamp to break ties.

sections.title: Status Replies
sections.content:
The REQUEST-STATUS property reports how a REPLY, COUNTER or DECLINECOUNTER went. If it is absent, code 2.0 (success) MUST be assumed. Codes are hierarchical numbers: the 2.x codes are successes with some caveat, for example 2.1 (fallback taken on a property value) and 2.2 (invalid property ignored). Code 4.0 means an event conflict because the date and time are busy, and 5.0 to 5.3 mean the request is unsupported or scheduling is not available.

When several REQUEST-STATUS properties appear, the first digit must agree within one component, so 2.xx and 5.xx cannot be mixed there. Across components, if any would have a 5.xx code then either all do or the property is left out of the others, and the same rule then applies to 3.xx. 2.xx and 4.xx may appear in different components.

The RFC creates a new IANA registry for REQUEST-STATUS values, initialized with the codes it defines, and adds the eight method names to the iCalendar METHOD registry.
sections.plainLanguage: Every answer can carry a little code that says how it went: worked, worked with a small catch, clashes with something else, or cannot be done here. With no code, the answer means it worked.

sections.title: Partial Implementations and Fallbacks
sections.content:
An application that supports iTIP does not have to support all of it. Section 5 says how methods and properties SHOULD fall back when a feature is missing. If a method or property is not addressed there, it may be ignored.

For events, PUBLISH, REPLY, CANCEL and REFRESH are required, and a system that does not do REQUEST falls back to treating it as PUBLISH. A system without recurrence support that receives ADD replies with REQUEST-STATUS 2.8 and schedules a single component. A system without COUNTER replies that it is not supported. For journal entries, unsupported methods may be ignored but the status 3.14, unsupported capability, MUST be returned.

Latency also matters on store-and-forward transports. A CANCEL may arrive before its REQUEST, so messages that cannot be correlated and have a non-zero sequence number are suggested to be held rather than discarded; implementations MAY age them out. An Organizer may also get a REPLY from a delegate it never invited, and it can accept it or hold it until the delegator's reply arrives.
sections.plainLanguage: A calendar program does not have to know every trick. The note says what simpler programs should do instead, such as treating an invitation as a plain announcement.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
iTIP is abstract, so the transport binding is responsible for authentication and encryption. Transport bindings MUST provide a way to authenticate the sender's identity and to protect the privacy and integrity of the data. Where the information is sensitive and attack is likely, iTIP transactions SHOULD be encrypted and authenticated.

The RFC lists specific threats: spoofing the Organizer to change or cancel an item, spoofing an Attendee to alter their ATTENDEE parameters, replacing the Organizer without agreement, eavesdropping on clear-text iCalendar data, flooding a calendar with requests that block all free time, and unauthorized REFRESH requests from people who are not Attendees.

Calendar systems SHOULD warn users of Organizer changes, offer controls to limit acceptable sources and volume, and let users decide on suspicious REFRESH requests. On privacy, an Organizer who does not want Attendees to see each other can send each Attendee a separate message listing only that Attendee.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone could pretend to be the host and cancel your party, so the delivery method has to prove who sent each message. Calendars should also let you say whose invitations you will accept so nobody can fill your whole day.
